33827052.extract:
### Early life
Dobbertin was born in Berlin, Germany, on 28 August 1882. Little is documented about his early education or training in photography, but by his early twenties, he had developed skills in the field. In 1903, at the age of 21, he emigrated to German East Africa, a colony established by the German Empire in the 1880s that encompassed present-day Tanzania, Burundi, and Rwanda. He settled in Dar es Salaam, the colonial capital, where he established himself as a commercial photographer.

### Career in German East Africa
From 1903 onward, Dobbertin operated as a photographer and publisher in German East Africa, founding book and art shops in Dar es Salaam, Tanga, and Moshi. His work focused on producing postcards, photograph albums, and prints that captured daily life in the colony. These included street scenes, colonial infrastructure such as hospitals and fortresses, indigenous communities, and natural landscapes. For example, one album from around 1905 features platinum prints of Tanga, showing urban development and local architecture.

Dobbertin also documented big game hunts and wildlife, with one 1910 album containing 48 images of animals like lions, elephants, and rhinos. Other collections from 1910–1911 depict African people engaged in activities such as transporting goods, village life, and fishing. His photographs often reflected a European colonial perspective, emphasizing exploration and resource exploitation. By 1910, he had published works like *Landschaftsbilder aus Deutsch-Ost-Afrika*, a 24-page collection of landscape images.

His business, Kunstverlag Walther Dobbertin, produced series of postcards and albums that were sold commercially, contributing to the visual representation of the colony in Germany and beyond.

### World War I
With the outbreak of World War I in 1914, Dobbertin joined the German colonial forces under General Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck. As the only known photographer documenting the German side of the East African Campaign, he captured images of askari (African soldiers in German service), military operations, and the harsh terrain. His photographs included scenes of skirmishes, troop movements, and daily military life, providing a rare visual record of the guerrilla warfare that characterized the campaign.

Dobbertin served until 1916, when he was captured by British forces. He was interned as a prisoner of war in India until his release after the war's end in 1918. Some of his negatives and photographs from this period were later preserved, though questions remain about how they were transported back to Germany during his internment.

### Post-war career
After his release, Dobbertin returned to Germany, where his colonial assets had been expropriated under the Treaty of Versailles. He settled in Wiedenhof (now part of Jesteburg, Lower Saxony) and reopened a bookshop and photography business. In the 1930s, he compiled and published collections of his East African photographs. Notable works include *Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbecks* (1932), a book of photogravures with 119 plates depicting the East African Campaign, and *Schwarz-Weiss-Rot Über Ost-Afrika* (1933), featuring 96 plates from his images.

During the Nazi era, Dobbertin was a member of the Sturmabteilung (SA), a paramilitary wing of the Nazi Party, and served as a district leader in the Reich Colonial Association, an organization promoting German colonial interests. Due to these affiliations, his business license was revoked by Allied authorities in 1945 following World War II. The license was later restored, allowing him to continue operating his bookshop until 1960.

### Death
Dobbertin died on 12 January 1961 in Jesteburg, Germany, at the age of 78.

### Legacy
Dobbertin's photographs are preserved in several institutions, including the Bundesarchiv in Germany, which holds his personal papers documenting colonial life in German East Africa. Collections also exist at Yale University's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Northwestern University's Melville J. Herskovits Library of African Studies, and the New York Public Library's Photographers' Identities Catalog.

His work has been used in historical research, such as studies of environmental changes in the Usambara Mountains and representations of colonial cities like Bagamoyo. Reprints of his books, including a 2005 English-German edition of *Lettow-Vorbeck's Soldiers*, have made his images accessible to modern audiences. While his photographs offer valuable historical documentation, they also reflect the biases of colonial-era imagery, focusing on European achievements and often portraying African subjects through a lens of otherness.

# Conditions Governing Use 

The Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa is the physical property of the 

Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University. Literary rights, including copyright, belong 

to the authors or their legal heirs and assigns. For further information, consult the appropriate curator. 

# Preferred Citation 

Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa. General Collection, Beinecke Rare 

Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University. 

# Processing Information 

Collections are processed to a variety of levels, depending on the work necessary to make them usable, 

their perceived research value, the availability of sta, competing priorities, and whether or not further 

accruals are expected. The library attempts to provide a basic level of preservation and access for all 

collections, and does more extensive processing of higher priority collections as time and resources 

permit. 

This collection received a basic level of processing, including rehousing and minimal organization. 

This finding aid may be updated periodically to account for new acquisitions to the collection or 

revisions in arrangement and description. 

Information included in the Content Description note and Collection Contents section is drawn 

from information supplied with the collection and from an initial survey of the contents. Portions 

of description for this collection have been directly repurposed from description supplied with the 

collection upon its receipt. Folder titles appearing in the contents list below are often based on those 

provided by the creator or previous custodian. Titles have not been verified against the contents of the 

folders in all cases. Otherwise, folder titles are supplied by sta during initial processing. 

Upon receipt, the collection was titled "From Cape to Cairo collection," as assigned by Humphrey 

Winterton and Maggs Brothers. The collection title was changed during processing in 2020. 

# Scope and Contents 

This collection consists of photograph albums, loose photographs, memorabilia and published material 

that document a European colonialist perspective of Africa and Egypt, and document both African peoples 

and European colonizers. Locations depicted in the photographs include Cameroon, Dar es Salaam, Egypt, 

Kenya, Namibia, Sudan, Tanga, Zambia, other regions throughout Africa, as well as some in Europe. 

Identified photographers in this collection include Alfredo Augusto Freire de Andrade, Walther Dobbertin, 

Paul Karl Lieberenz, and Carl von Vincenti. The bulk of photographs in the collection are created by 

unidentified photographers. 

# Arrangement 

Organized into seven series: I. Southern Africa, 1890 - 1929. II. Central Africa, circa 1918. III. East Africa, 1887 -

2005. IV. West Africa, 1880 - 1934. V. North Africa, 1904 - 1935. VI. Travel in Africa and Egypt, 1910 - 1920. VII. 

Colonial documentation of Africa, 1910 - 1933.

# Series I: Southern Africa, 1890–1929 

This series contains photograph albums and photographs documenting African colonial subjects, German 

colonialists, as well as wildlife in locations including Lourenco Marques, Transvaal, and Namibia. Also

Material is arranged alphabetically by subject.

This group of 50 mounted photographs contains images that document the 

delineation of the border between British and Portuguese territories in South 

East Africa, namely Portuguese-held Lourenco Marques and the Transvaal. 

Photographs include images of African colonial subjects, Lourenco Marques, the 

ocers of the Mozambique Expedition, the armoury, and the arrival of boats 

and Macequece. There are also images of the Portuguese fort and detachment, 

colonial headquarters, Beira, Freedom Church, Freedom Street Market, Sena in

b.  3 Namibia album of photographic reproductions by G. Lange 

This group of 60 photographic reproductions document German colonialists in 

Namibia. Included is a portrait of photographer G. Lange, along with inscriptions 

added to additional photographs by Lange. 

Founded in 1892 on the north coast of Namibia, Swakopmund quickly became 

the main harbour for the German colonialists in South West Africa. It received 

municipal status in 1909. The sketch map and many of the photographic images 

show the transport, principally rail, and route from the port of Swakopmund to 

the inland capital of Windhuk. The photographs depict warehouse life, train and 

railway stations in Kubas, Abbabis, Karibib, and Kaiser Wilhelmsberg. Images 

document scenes of the Schutztruppen arriving by ship, in parades, on patrol, and 

in combat scenes.

copies published by Battery Press Inc. of Nashville, Tennessee in 2005.

b.  13  Schwarz-Weiss-Rot Uber Ost-Afrika  by Walther Dobbertin 

First edition. Ninety-six plates in photogravure after photographs by 

Walther Dobbertin. Published by Sponholtz-Verlag, Hannover, 1933. 

1933 

b.  16  Tanga photograph album by Walther Dobbertin 

This album of 12 platinum photographs depicts the city of Tanga, including 

street scenes, the hospital, African huts, an old fortress, and the road to the 

cemetery. The cover of the album reads, "12 Bilder aus Deutsch-Ost-Afrika 

vom Kunstverlage Walther Dobbertin. Daressalam and Tanga D.O. Afrika, 

Serie IV. Tanga" 

circa 1905 

Unidentified photographers 

This series contains photograph albums and photographs by unidentified 

photographers. Locations depicted include Aden, Dar es Salaam, Egypt, Ethiopia, 

Kenya, Kilindini, Port Amelia, Rwanda, Saranda, Tanganyika, Uganda, Yemen, and 

Zanzibar. Subjects documented include street scenes, city views, architecture, 

German troops, African colonial troops, African colonial subjects, and colonial 

expeditions. 

Material is arranged alphabetically by subject. 

1887–1919 

b.  17  Aden and Zanzibar photographs 

This group of 14 photographs depicts Zanzibar and Aden from 1890 to 1910. 

Images include a view of Zanzibar harbour, a group photograph featuring 

Sayyid Hamad bin Thuwaini with four African advisors, Lloyd Mathews, the 

Prime Minister of Zanzibar, and Sir Arthur Harding. Other images include a 

street scene in Dar es Salaam, Sultan's palace, Boma of Bagamoyo, the clis 

at Aden harbour, and German soldiers, hunters, and ocers. 

1890-1910 

Walther Dobbertin (continued) 

Page  10  of  20 Series III: East Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  18  Dar es Salaam, Kilindini, Port Amelia, and Saranda photograph album 

Kilindini became a significant harbour with the commencement of the 

construction of the Uganda Railway. HMS Challenger was moved to the East 

Africa Station in 1915 in order to take part in operations against the German 

ship SMS Königsberg in the Rufijii River. 

This album contains 160 photographs from August and September, 1916. The 

images depict several ports along the East African coast during World War 

I. The first part of the album documents Kilindini, the port at Mombasa, and 

includes images of the HMS Challenger and Vengeance, and damage to the 

docks. 

The album includes images of Mombasa itself, Dar es Salaam and Saranda 

in Tanganyika, and to the south a photo of Port Amelia in Mozambique. 

In addition there are views of African dhows, dwellings and farms, the 

Governor's residence and much of the infrastructure on the coast. 

1916 August -

September 

b.  19  East Africa, Egypt, Kenya, and Yemen photograph album 

This photograph album contains 163 images with individual, handwritten 

captions taken in Dar es Salaam, Aden, Lindi, Massassi, Nyangao, Zanzibar, 

Tanga, Mombasa, Suez and Port Said. The photographs depict naval craft, 

markets, village life, street scenes, and city views. Individuals documented 

include both German and colonial troops. The album also includes an image 

of a funeral for a German soldier, which bears Carl Vincenti's stamp in the 

bottom right hand corner. 

1905-1906 

b.  20  East Africa photograph albums 

2 Folders 

These two photograph albums contain 96 photographs of Dar es Salaam. 

The albums are bound, and titled, "Bilder aus Deutsch-Ostafrika." One album 

has a corresponding list of photograph captions. The first album depicts 

gatherings of African colonial subjects, including archery competitions, 

groups of women, dancing, and ceremonies. 

The second album appears to document an expedition primarily around 

Tanganyika. Images depict boats and canoes, porters transporting luggage 

and other supplies across rivers and over land to a series of villages 

in Tabora, Zanzibar as well as Dar es Salaam. The album also includes 

photographs of pottery production in Burundi and a tea plantation in 

Rwanda. 

1910 

b.  21  East Africa photograph album 

This album contains 144 photographs with individual handwritten captions 

on the eve of the World War I. Images depict Dar es Salaam including the 

sea trade, ocean liners and barges in the harbour, and African fisherman in 

small sailboats. This album also contains photographs that depict a series 

of houses in Dar es Salaam and the surrounding regions of Lindi, Morogoro, 

Sekenke, Singida, and Ngago, including a workhouse, the Governor's house, 

and European and African dwellings. Also included are images that appear to 

follow a train journey out into the countryside, including many photographs 

of African colonial subjects, agriculture, mission stations as well as the 

occasional images of the expedition itself. 

circa 1912 

Unidentified photographers (continued) 

Page  11  of  20 Series III: East Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  22  East Africa and Egypt photograph album 

This album contains 103 photographs, cigarette cards, and other ephemera. 

It appears the owner of the album served on the SMS Königsberg. Early in the 

album there is an image of a group of five ocers from the ship. Königsberg 

was the lead ship in the German Imperial Navy, and is best known for service 

during the First World War. 

The album includes three panoramas of Dar es Salaam, as well as depictions 

of the harbor, African dwellings, colonial bridges, and African porters 

transporting goods. The album also contains photographs of the Maasai 

people and African colonial subjects. The images include dancing, hair 

dressing, jewellery, clothing, children, bathing, grinding wheat, tribal 

councils, and a series of colonial encounters. The album closes with a few 

photographs of Egypt, a picture of Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck and Schnee in 

Berlin, ephemera relating to Cairo and East Africa and two images of soldiers 

in Nazi uniforms. Several photographs depict the racist practice of blackface. 

1914-1919 

b.  23  Italian Eritrea Expedition photograph album 

This album of the Italian Eritrea Expedition contains 115 photographs with 

handwritten captions and a large folding 1895 colour lithograph map of 

Eritrea in the rear pocket. 

This album documents the arrival of Italian colonialists in Northern Ethiopia 

at the beginning of the Italy-Abyssinia war, 1887-1889. The album also 

includes images of Dogali, where Ras Alula, the Ethiopian general, achieved 

victory over the Italians in January 1887. 

The album contains images that depict Suez, Port Said and the Canal, the 

pyramids and the Sphinx. There are thirty photos of Massawa and its port. 

Other images include vaccinations being administered to African patients, 

group portraits of the medical corps, ocers, African commanders, military 

installations, Assab, Otumlo, the Swedish Mission at Moncullo, Dogali and 

the camp of Ras Alula, Fort Borelli, Fort Victor Emanuele, and Massawa 

Saati. The album concludes with images of of families, soldiers, housing, and 

villages. 

1887–1895 

b.  13  Kenya, Uganda, and Tanganyika photograph album 

This album of Kenya, Uganda, and Tanganyika during World War I contains 

123 photographs with handwritten captions. Although the East Africa 

Campaign had eectively finished by November 1917, the German army 

remained active a year later. Taken in mid-1918, the images contained 

in this album depict the medical facilities in East Africa at the time. The 

photographs include hospital sta and British and Kenyan soldiers, many 

of whom are identified by name. The Carrier Hospital at Lindi (Tanganyika) 

and the Sanitorium at Kijabe (Kenya) are well documented. The album 

also includeds images of Dar es Salaam and Lindi, waterbuck and eland at 

Bukoba, Chania Falls at Thika, the remains of a German wireless at Mwanza, 

a German fort at Mwanza, Bukoba, Entebbe, CMS Hospital at Kampala, the 

Nile at Jinja and Victoria Nyanza, SS Ebani, and the fort at Mombasa, B.E.A. 

1918 

b.  24  Panoramic photograph of Rwanda by unidentified photographer (Vater) 

This four print panorama looks toward the three volcanoes in the Virunga 

Mountains from what appears to be a tea plantation. At a conference 

in Brussels in 1890, Germany was granted both Rwanda and Burundi in 

exchange for relinquishing all claims to Uganda. The photograph is inscribed 

with the name "Vater." 

1909 April 19 

Unidentified photographers (continued) 

Page  12  of  20 Series IV: West Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

# Series IV: West Africa, 1880–1934 

This series contains photograph albums and photographs depicting locations including Cameroon, Lomé, 

Portugal, Senegal, and Togo. Images document German plantations, trains, African peoples, landscapes, 

German colonialists, and architecture. 

Material is arranged alphabetically by subject. 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  25  Cameroon photograph album by Paul Karl Lieberenz 

This album, titled "Nord-Kamerun" of Cameroon contain 66 photographs taken by 

the German colonial photographer Paul Karl Lieberenz. The album includes four 

panoramic photographs, a colour illustration marking the German plantations in 

Cameroon, mainly palm oil, cocoa, banana, and gum, as well as a small sketch map. 

Photographs in the albums document Lieberenz's travels in North Cameroon in 

1933-34. Images include colonial depictions of the life and customs of Indigenous 

tribes native to Cameroon, including those living in Pirate Islands, and towns and 

villages of Buea, Mbemi, Bali, Babanki Tungo, Babungo, Banso, and Kumbo. 

Other locations and scenes depicted in the photographs include Mount 

Cameroon, the seaside city of Victoria (Limbe), Bota Island, Fernando Po (Bioko, 

Bioco), Bamenda (Abakwa and Mankon Town), the volcanic landscape of Babanki 

Tungoh, the historic fortress of Bamenda, the residence of von Puttkamer in Buea, 

a Mamfe tomb, banana plantations in Tiko, a Banso-warrior, ceremonial dance, a 

crowded local market, Mbemi women preparing palm oil, an African man climbing 

up a coco tree, skilled woodcarvers of Babanki Tungo, African people crossing the 

Mungo River, and glimpses of steelmakers extracting iron in the charcoal ovens. 

1933-1934 

b.  26–27  Cameroon and Togo photographs 

10 Folders 

This group of 98 photographs of Cameroon and Togo includes mounted 

photographs, a three-print panorama, and postcards. Many have German captions 

in pencil on the verso. The images depict trains and passengers at a station, 

scenes at sea, including one of Monrovia, rural scenes with people, and colonialists 

and African people. Of the 43 larger images, seven are identified on the verso as 

being of Togo and 29 as Cameroon, with the remaining seven unidentified. The 

panorama shows the mission in Nyasono in south-west Cameroon. 

Other images depict landscapes, animals, and infrastructure such as bridges and 

railways, ships and boats on the Atlantic, waterways, rivers, and harbors. Also 

included is a glass plate negative box that was used to house photographs. 

1897-1905 

b.  27  Lomé, Togo panoramic photograph 

This folding nine-image panorama of Lomé, Togo stretches from the coast to 

the medical center. Thirty-four buildings are numbered including the post oce, 

the government school, factories, military barracks, and the train station. The 

panorama is housed in a bound book, and titled, "Panorama von Lome, Hauptitadt 

des Togogebietes" 

1905 

Page  13  of  20 Series IV: West Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  28  Luanda, Cabinda, Sao Thome, Costa d'Ouro and Sao Miguel photograph album 

This album contains 92 photographs. The album pages have been removed from 

the album binding. Images depict colonial buildings in Cabinda and Luanda, such 

as the governor's residence, military barracks, the hospital, a pharmacy, bridges, 

a cocoa factory, the Roca de Santa Virginia Mission, and views of Costa d'Ouro, 

Funchal, Madeira, Sao Miguel, and Sao Thome. 

Photographs also depict group images of African people from Sao Thome, Cabinda 

and Malarige, as well as people harvesting sugar cane, musicians, and an inland 

expeditionary group. 

circa 1880s 

b.  27  Senegal photographs 

This group of 14 photographs depicts the Bassari people, goods being transported 

across the Hamansu River, Ho Station, Bimbila Station, Misahohe Station, farming 

in Uapuli, a view over Bassari, the construction of a hut, a group of Islamic school 

students, views of Kamanji and Atakpame, and the chief of Apai and his followers. 

undated 

b.  29  Togo photograph album 

This album of Togo contains 57 photographs documenting the German colonial 

period from 1910-1912. Also included is a postcard of Lomé and an original color 

map, marking the German protectorate. 

The album includes photographs of Togo, featuring towns and villages of Lomé, 

Sokodé, Banjeli, Palimé (Kpalimé), Misahöhe, and Sebe. The images reflect the 

life and environment of African people in Togo during the colonial period and 

show views from the port of Lomé, train tracks, and a German colonial station 

in Missahohé. Individuals and subjects depicted include an African woman with 

scarification, women miners of Banjeli, iron-smelting ovens, market scenes, views 

of Mount Agou (Mount Baumann) from the village, dam construction, colonial 

ocials and their families, German Colonial Police, and African interpreters in 

European suits. 

1910-1912 

Page  14  of  20 Series V: North Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

# Series V: North Africa, 1904–1935 

This series contains photograph albums documenting locations including Egypt, France, Italy, and Sudan. 

Images document African peoples, military troops, street scenes, and big game hunting. 

Material is arranged chronologically. 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  30  Egypt and Sudan photograph albums by Henry Maitland Wilson 

Field Marshall Lord Henry Maitland Wilson, G.C.B., G.B.E., D.S.O. (1881-1964) 

attended Eton and Sandhurst before being commissioned into the Rifle Brigade 

as a 2nd Lieutenant in May 1900. Nicknamed "Jumbo", Wilson's military career 

included service in the Boer War and World War I, before attaining the rank of 

General and overseeing operations in the Middle East and Mediterranean. 

Between 1939 and 1944, he held various commands in North Africa and the Middle 

East when he succeeded General Eisenhower as Supreme Allied Commander of 

the Mediterranean Theatre. He was a confidant of Winston Churchil and was 

made Field Marshall in 1944. Three years later he became Chief of the British Joint 

Sta Mission in Washington D.C. where his friendship with Eisenhower prospered 

(to the extent that Eisenhower provided an introduction to Wilson's volume of 

wartime memoirs). In 1944 he became Baron Wilson of Libya and of Stowlangtoft. 

These photograph albums document a hunting trip in Sudan and Egypt and 

contain 163 photographs with captions. One album is signed "HM Wilson Rifle 

Brigade" on the front pastedown. 

These albums record a hunting trip made with Field Marshall Lord Henry Maitland 

Wilson and fellow soldiers along the White Nile. Included are photographs of 

African communities, including the Shilluk people, the Baggara, the Nuer people, 

and the Dinka people. Other images depict big game hunting, fellow travellers, as 

well as markets, the boats on which they sailed, and life along the shores of the 

Nile. 

1904-1905 

b.  31  Egypt photograph album by G.A. Chadburn 

3 Folders 

This album of Egypt contains 78 photographs, 65 silk regimental arms, newspaper 

clippings, and two cotton maps of the Dardanelles, and of central Europe. 

Egypt allied itself with the Central Powers at the outbreak of war and these 

images present a rare insight to this arena. British troops struck early in order to 

secure the Anglo-Persian pipeline and withstood a counter attack in February 

1915. The album appears to belong to G.A. Chadburn from Stockport, whose card 

is taped to the front pastedown. There is also an image of soldiers from Cheadle 

Hulme, which is part of Stockport. 

The album includes images of troops in Cairo, Alexandria, Hadra Prison, Sakhara 

and Ismailia in the early months of the war. There is a selection of images 

featuring artillery, inspection lines, the Australian camp at Giza, US ships at 

Alexandria, and bridge building. 

Other images depict individuals traveling throughout Egypt, a picnic on the Nile 

on Easter Sunday, 1915, Egyptian fruit sellers, fishermen, and coast guards. The 

final photographs are of a military hospital in Reading. The newspaper clippings all 

relate to the Dardanelles campaign, particularly Gallipoli. 

circa 1910s 

Page  15  of  20 Series V: North Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  32  Egypt World War I photograph album 

This album contains 400 photographs documenting British troops in Egypt during 

World War I. The photographer was based in the British camp at Beni Salama, 

which is situated about 60 kilometers north west of Cairo on the western edge 

of the Nile delta. Photographs depict Egyptian people, firing practice, camp 

accommodations in the desert (tents, latrines), troops riding horseback and 

camels, meals, feluccas on the Nile, the sphinx and pyramids at Giza, street scenes 

in Cairo, the Muhammad Ali Mosque, and the ancient monuments at Luxor. The 

group portraits are of the Ocers of the Woolwich Sub-Command London AA 

Defences. 

1916 

b.  33  Egypt, France, Italy, and Sudan photograph album 

This album of Egypt, Sudan, Italy, Sicily and France contains 202 photographs. 

The annotations are detailed and provide information on the various ports and 

cities encountered. The bulk of this annotated album comprises photographs 

taken in Egypt and in Sudan as the photographer appears to have travelled down 

the Nile on the ship Straithaird. African communities represented include the 

Dinka people, the Shilluk people, the Nuer people, and the Bari people. Towns or 

ports documented include Taormina, Port Said, Port Sudan, Melut, Malakal, Sambe, 

Malek and Khartoum, before the photographer ventures back to northern Italy 

and the south of France, ending finally in Provence. 

1933–1935 

Page  16  of  20 Series VI: Travel in Africa and Egypt  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

# Series VI: Travel in Africa and Egypt, 1910–1920 

This series contains photograph albums and photographs documenting locations including Algeria, Egypt, 

Ghana, Kenya, and other locations in Africa. Images depict big game hunting, European colonialists, African 

colonial subjects, and architecture. 

Material is arranged alphabetically by subject. 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  34–35  Africa and Egypt photograph albums 

These albums document a trip from Southern Africa to Cairo and contains 576 

photographs. The opening images in the first album are of Zambezi River at 

Victoria Falls. Images in the albums depict a big game hunting safari undertaken 

on both sides of the river in both Northern and Southern Rhodesia (present day 

Zambia and Zimbabwe). Images include the hunting party which consisted of 

the European colonialists and African people, as well as the game that was killed, 

including elephant, bualo, a lion and lioness, zebra, warthog, wild boar, hyena, gnu 

and antelope. Included is a series of photographs of young rhinos on a farm being 

hand-reared and bottle-fed, as well as young bualo being loaded into a crate and 

the onto a rear of a truck. 

Photographs in the second album depicts African people and European 

colonialists on big game hunts. Other images document an Ocean voyage, and 

scenes depicting the Sphinx and the Great Pyramid of Giza. The end of the album 

depictcts large European-style houses, ostriches and pelicans in cages. The 

remainder of the album include more images of Cairo and Giza, as well as images 

of individuals. 

circa 1920 

b.  31  Algeria, Ghana, and Kenya photographs 

This group of five photographs includes one of Algeria, inscribed, "Alger: La 

Kasbah: Rue de la Mer Rouge." Two other photographs are inscribed with "Accra" 

on the verso and depict the docks of Ghana. Two other photographs depict groups 

of Bantu peoples of Western Kenya. 

circa 1910 

Page  17  of  20 Series VII: Colonial documentation of Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

# Series VII: Colonial documentation of Africa, 1910–1933 

This series contains primarily printed material created by European colonialists about Africa. Included 

are volumes of photographic reproductions, published material, and a photograph album. The material 

documents how a colonial perspective of Africa was produced and distributed to a European audience. 

Material is arranged chronologically. 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  36–37  Die Deutschen Kolonien 

Two volume sets of bound photographic reproductions, with additional mounted 

photographic reproductions. The first set is divided into the following volumes: 

I. Togo, II. Kamerun, III. Deutsch-Südwestafrika. The second set contains the 

following volumes: I. Deutsch-Ost-Afrika, II. Kaiser-Wilhelmsland und die Inselwelt 

im Stillen Ozean, III. Samoa, IV. Kiautschou. 

All the photographic reproductions and plates are the work of three 

photographers: Dr Robert Lohmeyer, Bruno Marquardt and Eduard Kiewning. 

Printing was done by the Institute for Colour Photography, Carl Weller, Berlin. 

circa 1910 

b.  31  Deutschlands Kolonien by Willy Scheele 

First edition by Weller and Hüttich, Berlin. 1912. 63 of the 80 images and 124 pages 

of the text are devoted to the German colonies in Africa including Togo, Kamerun, 

Deutsch-Südwestafrika, and Deutsch-Ostafrika. 

1912 

b.  31  Farbfotografien aus den Deutschen Kolonien by Willy Scheel 

2 Folders 

48 color oset lithography reproductions with printed captions. Foreword by 

Dr. Scheel, including the narrative, "Overview of the German Colonies." The 48 

illustrations have been selected from the 80 which are included in Dr. Scheel's 

book. Though primarily devoted to German colonies in Africa, this set of images 

provides photographs of Togo, Cameroon, German Southwest Africa, German 

East Africa, New Guinea, Caroline Islands, the Bismarck Archipelago, Samoa, and 

Kiatschou Bay. 

All of the photographic reproductions and plates are the work of three 

photographers: Dr Robert Lohmeyer, Bruno Marquardt and Eduard Kiewning. 

Publication is by Carl Weller of the Institute for Colour Photography, Berlin. 

1913 

b.  38  Das Kolonial Wirtschaftliche Komitee Berlin Kolonial Ausstellung By Paul 

Lieberenz 

The Colonial Economic Development Committee of Berlin was founded in the late 

nineteenth century for the purpose of finding and identifying tropical plants and 

agricultural crops which could be commercially exploited. It mounted numerous 

expeditions for this purpose, frequently to remote areas not previously visited 

by Europeans. Its work was greatly hampered after Germany's loss of its colonies 

during and after the First World War. In the 1920s Germany was in political 

and economic turmoil and, by the end of 1930, parliamentary democracy had 

eectively given way to an increasingly authoritarian regime with the National 

Socialists gaining ground. Against this background, the politicians were looking 

for ways to restore Germany's influence abroad, including the former colonies. 

Original commemorative photographic album produced by Paul Lieberenz for 

the German Colonial Exhibition held in Berlin in May 1933. The album contains 

14 photographs, including a printed introductory essay by the Committee's 

Chairman, Dr. h. c. A. Drehn. 

There is documentation of the racist practice of including live humans in 

anthropological displays, featuring people from Africa who were brought over to 

Berlin to be used in the exhibition. 

1933 

Page  18  of  20 Series VII: Colonial documentation of Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

Container  Description  Date 

Other images include general views of the exhibition, including a thatched stand 

of the "Frauenbund der Deutschen Kolonialgesellschaft," a display for "Frauverein 

vom Roten Kreuz Für Deutsche Über See," a display of objects of the Südsee 

Gebeite, a display of Deutsch Ost Afrika which features agricultural produce, 

Masai artifacts and a model of an Askari, a display for Deutsch Süd West Afrika 

comprising mainly of photographs and displays in glass cases, and the display of 

Kamerun and Togo featuring carved wooden objects such as stools, woven straw 

hats, fans, and textiles.

GEN MSS 1606

Walther Dobbertin

**Walther Dobbertin** (* 1882 in Berlin; † 12. Januar 1961 in Jesteburg-Wiedenhof) war ein deutscher Fotograf und 1906 - 1915 in Ostafrika tätig. [[1]](http://kilimanjaro.bplaced.net/wiki/index.php?title=Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-wikipedia-0)

**Walther Dobbertin und der Kilimanjaro**
-----------------------------------------

*    1903 wanderte Walther Dobbertin nach Deutsch-Ostafrika aus. In Daressalam, Tanga und Moshi gründete er Buch- und Kunsthandlungen. Er entwickelte sich zum bedeutendsten Fotografen Deutsch-Ostafrikas. Nach dem Ausbruch des Ersten Weltkrieges war er der einzige Fotograf, der die Geschehnisse auf deutscher Seite dokumentierte. [[1]](http://kilimanjaro.bplaced.net/wiki/index.php?title=Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-wikipedia-0)
*    Dobbertin war als Fotograf in den Jahren 1906 bis 1915 in Deutsch-Ostafika tätig. Seine Aufnahmen stellen für zahlreiche Siedlungsgebiete des heutigen Tanzania oft die erste, z.T. hervorragende Bilddokumentation dar. [[2]](http://kilimanjaro.bplaced.net/wiki/index.php?title=Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-1)
*    Walther Dobbertin war als erster und einziger Berufsfotograf von 1906 bis 1914, dann als Landsturmmann bis 1918, in Ostafrika tätig. [[3]](http://kilimanjaro.bplaced.net/wiki/index.php?title=Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-2)
*    1916 geriet Dobbertin als Mitglied der deutschen Schutztruppe in englische Gefangenschaft. Bei Kriegsende wurden die Deutschen aus Ostafrika ausgewiesen und enteignet. Der Frau Dobbertins, Alwine, gelang es aber, die fotografischen Platten ihres Mannes außer Landes zu schmuggeln. Nach seiner Entlassung aus der Gefangenschaft kehrte Dobbertin nach Deutschland zurück und zog nach Wiedenhof, heute ein Ortsteil von Jesteburg, südlich von Hamburg. Dort eröffnete er erneut eine Buchhandlung. [[1]](http://kilimanjaro.bplaced.net/wiki/index.php?title=Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-wikipedia-0)
*    In seiner Zeit in Deutsch-Ostafrika enstanden auch viele Fotos vom Kilimanjaro und seiner unmittelbaren Umgebung. Diese Fotos sind großartige Dokumente mit denen man auch den Verfall der Gletscher am Kibo nachvollziehen kann.

### **Lettow-Vorbeck's Soldiers**, Walther Dobbertin, 1932, 128 Seiten

*    Die Soldaten Lettow-Worbecks: ein Buch von deutschem Wehrwillen und deutscher Waffenehre: 120 künstlerische Kupfertiefdrucke nach Aufnahmen aus dem Weltkriege in Deutsch-Ostafrika 
*    Reprint 2005, 143 Seiten, The Battery Press, [ISBN 089839340X](http://kilimanjaro.bplaced.net/wiki/index.php?title=Spezial:ISBN-Suche/089839340X), [ISBN 9780898393408](http://kilimanjaro.bplaced.net/wiki/index.php?title=Spezial:ISBN-Suche/9780898393408), bei Amazon.com: 

Originally published in 1932 in Germany as Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbeck, this is a dual language (English/German) reprint edition. Dobbertin was a commercial photographer in German East Africa prior to World War I. When all German men were mobilized in August 1914 to defend the colony, Dobbertin became, in effect, the only combat photographer on the German side. He performed this function until his own capture in 1916. Lettow-Vorbeck's Soldiers contains 120 of the best of his photos for this campaign. It is particularly important for showing the service of black German soldiers in German East Africa. [[4]](http://kilimanjaro.bplaced.net/wiki/index.php?title=Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-3)

Bagamoyo Imperial and Actual: Representation of the First Capital of German East Africa in Colonial Postcards and in the Works of Walter Dobbertin
==================================================================================================================================================

#### **Author**:

Anastasia Banshchikova

#### Abstract:

In recent decades, items of colonial photography, including those dedicated to German East Africa, have become the subject of research by historians and anthropologists. Many of the photographs eventually became postcards issued to introduce newly conquered territories to the citizens of the empire, to a lesser extent their population, culture and way of life, and to a greater extent those achievements (both real and imaginary) that the metropolis had brought. This included military stations, churches, missions, infrastructure (railways, train stations, lighthouses), askari troops recruited from local population, etc. On these postcards we can see various species of acacias and palm trees, numerous Araberstrasse and Kaiserstrasse streets, monuments to the emperor and chancellor, ships in the Dar es Salaam bay, “native beauty” and “native quarters”. On the one hand, postcards reflect what colonizers wanted to display before their homeland, on the other they reflect what this homeland itself wanted to see, e.g. images of exotic hot tropics, successes of German administrators and troops. Postcards, being selected in their very plots and created for the propaganda purposes, depict German East Africa strictly deliberately and strictly as a colony.

Bagamoyo served as this colony’s capital for about two years. On postcards depicting the town we see the quintessence of the German military and administrative presence: this is tangible both in the choice of depicted objects (fort, boma, Wissmann’s monument in memory of soldiers who died during the suppression of the coastal uprising, meeting place of the colonial administration, etc.) and the frequency of these choices. Images of local residents on postcards are marginal, the “black quarter” is opposed to new European buildings, and the elements of the Arab-Swahili cultural component of Bagamoyo are not represented at all.

On the contrary, photography of Walter Dobbertin allows to have a look at Bagamoyo in the end of the 19th – the beginning of the 20th centuries in a much more complete and complicated way. He took photos of inhabitants of Bagamoyo with clear accent and opened vision – women, children, Arabs, Muslims in kanzu and kofias, without censoring either the phenotype or the cultural components of Islamic religion (mosque, Muslim cemetery, tea houses). It’s fascinating, because negative attitude toward Arabs and Islam is stressed throughout many German colonial narratives written by military and civil officers. The Arabs as “the first colonizers of the region”, i.e. predecessors of Germans themselves, almost never appear on the postcards, as well as Islam-associated objects like mosques or Muslim cemeteries. The article is concerned with this difference between postcards and photographs of Bagamoyo as the latter reveal what had been blind spots of official representation of colony’s first capital and give very personal and much more sincere vision offered by talented photographer Walter Dobbertin.

Originally published in 1932 in Germany as Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbeck, this is a dual language (English/German) reprint edition. Dobbertin was a commercial photographer in German East Africa prior to World War I. When all German men were mobilized in August 1914 to defend the colony, Dobbertin became, in effect, the only combat photographer on the German side. He performed this function until his own capture in 1916. Lettow-Vorbeck's Soldiers contains 120 of the best of his photos for this campaign. It is particularly important for showing the service of black German soldiers in German East Africa.

De Greene](https://www.amazon.com/gp/profile/amzn1.account.AFM7FFZONXC7GHJTW32FUUMSLKKQ/ref=cm_cr_dp_d_gw_tr?ie=UTF8) ##### [_5.0 out of 5 stars_ A Little-Known Chapter of World War I History in East Africa](https://www.amazon.com/gp/customer-reviews/R1PQ3BOBU6U7JQ/ref=cm_cr_dp_d_rvw_ttl?ie=UTF8) Reviewed in the United States on June 7, 2015 Format: Hardcover[Verified Purchase](https://www.amazon.com/gp/help/customer/display.html/ref=cm_cr_dp_d_rvw_avp?nodeId=G8UYX7LALQC8V9KA) A couple of decades ago, in a bookstore in East Africa, I found a book roughly entitled Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck: Prussian Lion of Africa. Von Lettow-Vorbeck's troops defeated in battles the English, the Britishers' Indian and Boer troops, and the Portuguese in skirmishes over large tracts of land. Lettow-Vorbeck was never captured. Eventually, he road through the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin with his remaining 100 men out of an original 3000, victors of 1000 battles. Recently, I wanted to refer to the book but couldn't find it in my rather large library. So I Googled Lettow-Vorbeck, the result being the present book. The book can be divided into two sections: text and photos. In turn, the text can be divided into two sections: a historical review and a biography of photographer Walther Dobbertin. The discussions in the historical review surprised me. Apparently, the Imperial government in Berlin carried little for German East Africa. When WWI broke out, the settlers were largely dependent on their own resourcefulness and toughness. Their weapons were obsolete. Yet the white Germans and their several thousand black African askaris and bearers were able to hold off or defeat several thousand of the enemy. The enemy paid a very high price in deaths and monetary costs. Dobbertin's biography discusses his ups and downs, including early success as a photographer in East Africa, becoming an English POW sent to India, becoming a book dealer and photographer back in Germany, and losing his license in 1945 because of SA membership. He never got back to East Africa. Fortunately, his plates and a film were acquired by the National Archives in Koblenz. There are120 artistic photoengravings of photographs. Some examples: scenes of Lake Victoria and Kilimanjaro of today's touristic fame, "artillery moves through the city" (looks like our Civil War cannon!), a self-built seaplane, and the tallest and shortest askaris in a field company. Fittingly, the frontispiece shows a youthful-looking General von Lettow-Vorbeck.

Now, what is the market for this book? Not immense, but it could include students of German and African history and world travelers. 19.title: V2FsdGhlciBEb2JiZXJ0aW4gcmFpc2VzIHF1ZXN0aW9ucw==
19.content:
Walther Dobbertin was a German photographer who spent time in East Africa before and during World War 1. Many of the photos we know of German askari were taken by Dobbertin.

Suprisingly, there doesn’t seem to be a biography of Walther. He was born in 1882, emigrated to German East Africa in 1903, served with the German army in East Africa during World War One until his capture in 1916. After being released as a prisoner of war, he returned to Germany where he died in 1961. There is a lovely photo of him [here](http://kilimanjaro.bplaced.net/wiki/index.php?title=Walther_Dobbertin).

What I find intriguing though, is that many of his war photos are dated 10/4/1918. I discovered this when completing the book [Zambia: The end of the Great War in Africa 1918-2018](https://gweaa.com/product/zambia-the-end-of-the-war-in-africa-25-november-1918-25-november-2018-gwaa/). We were, and still are, trying to identify [the British officer in a photo](https://ilo.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papeles:Bundesarchiv_Bild_146-2004-0094,_Paul_Emil_von_Lettow-Vorbeck_/(Mitte/).jpg) with von Lettow-Vorbeck and Georg Kraut. This particular photo is marked March 1918, although the commons licence notes March 1919, and to the credit of the [Bundesarchiv](https://www.bild.bundesarchiv.de/archives/barchpic/search/_1556878882/?search[view]=detail&search[focus]=1), it does not identify the photographer.

The photo and date pose some challenges:

– in March 1918, von Lettow Vorbeck was in Portuguese East Africa, so highly unlikely he’d be posing in a relaxed photo with a British staff officer.  
– it is most likely this photo was taken after the surrender/laying down of arms once the German officers had arrived in Dar es Salaam which places is between December 1918 and 5 February 1919. At this time, Dobbertin was in a prisoner of war camp somewhere having been taken prisoner in 1916.

The conclusion here is that someone other than Dobbertin must have taken this photo, a British soldier who gave a copy to von Lettow-Vorbeck? This seems the most likely explanation for how this got into the Bundesarchiv.

But what about the other photos Dobbertin took which are dated 4/1918? eg [1](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA3049,_Deutsch-Ostafrika,_Askari_beim_%C3%9Cbungsschie%C3%9Fen.jpg), [2](https://www.google.com/imgres?imgurl=https%3A%2F%2Fi.imgur.com%2FdXV91CK.jpg&imgrefurl=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.reddit.com%2Fr%2Fwwi%2Fcomments%2F2lkgkq%2Fwalther_dobbertin_askari_skirmish_in_german_east%2F&docid=0z1vAdCK-lmX7M&tbnid=c-47RStvYBUC0M%3A&vet=10ahUKEwjwkLXEjP_hAhVloXEKHbHyDBUQMwhBKAAwAA..i&w=800&h=565&itg=1&bih=730&biw=1525&q=walther%20dobbertin&ved=0ahUKEwjwkLXEjP_hAhVloXEKHbHyDBUQMwhBKAAwAA&iact=mrc&uact=8), [3](https://t.co/Gu6kKSSYQm)

*   Was Dobbertin part of a prisoner exchange which saw him return to Germany earlier than post-war?
*   Was he allowed to send his wife all these photos or negatives whilst a prisoner? Surely the British authorities would have wanted to see the photos themselves and possibly kept a copy – are these hidden away in an archive or private collection somwhere?
*   Did Dobbertin manage to give the negatives to one of the captains of a blockade runner who then was able to return to Germany via Portuguese East Africa?
*   Are these the dates the negatives were developed by Dobbertin in his prison camp, which were then later adopted by the Bundesarchiv when it catalogued the collection? eg 2 looks like it was taken at Tanga in 1914

Other questions which then come to mind:

*   Did Dobbertin only take photos for his own pursposes? or
*   were any of his photos used for intelligence purposes such as those taken by Cherry Kearton?

From the sample of photos available on the internet, it appears that none were taken for intelligence purposes, which begs the question, why?  
And then, the German photos referred to in the Bohill collection at [Hendon RAF Archive](https://www.rafmuseum.org.uk/research/default/archive-collection.aspx) – who were they taken by? And what did they consist of? And where are they now?

A sample of Dobbertin’s photos was published in 1932, [since reprinted](https://gweaa.com/product/lettow-vorbecks-soldiers/), but with the advent of the internet, [many can be found online](https://www.google.com/search?sa=X&q=walther+dobbertin&tbm=isch&source=lnms&ved=2ahUKEwjI5pe5jP_hAhVWUhUIHTOnCpMQsAR6BAgJEAE&biw=1525&bih=730#imgrc=E86WkPQtim76HM:) thanks to the Bundesarchiv’s accessibility policy.

Perhaps one day someone will consider investigating this man who has provided us with a fascinating collection of photos from the German colonial period in East Africa.

28.title: Bundesarchiv - Bilddatenbank
28.content:
The Federal Archives preserve approx. 12 million pictures, aerial photos and posters on German history. The earliest photographs date back to the year 1860. The main focus of the collection is on pictures documenting events and persons of German history. For investigating specific epochs, certain record groups will be of interest:

![Image 1: Bild 105 Personal papers Walther Dobbertin (=Nachlass Walther Dobbertin)](https://bild.bundesarchiv.de/device_barch/dev2/2020/01-17/98/e9/file78vxhgy7r1y16kj3nfm.jpg)

The photos mainly portray the life of German inhabitants of the colony German East Africa. They show political, socio-economic and military events. There are also a large number of landscape and family photographs. Pictures from the colonies German South West Africa and Kamerun, which are also part of this fonds, display similar motifs like those from German East Africa.

[All documents of this inventory](https://www.bild.bundesarchiv.de/dba/en/search/?topicid%5B%5D=dcx-dcxapi%3Atm_topic/thes_bestand_774u70q3fd5axdnnd48 "All documents of this inventory")

![Image 2: Bild 102 Aktuelle-Bilder-Centrale, Georg Pahl](https://bild.bundesarchiv.de/device_barch/dev1/2025/04-17/98/37/file808vzf96uf9kl1traxd.jpg)

Photographic records include important political events, public events and daily life in the Weimar Republic and the period of National Socialism from 1923 to 1936 (1946-1955). Besides political photographs (including foreign affairs) and photos of prominent individuals, the fonds also documents the following topics: Economy, transport, military, sport, culture and art, but also natural disasters and accidents. The pictures were taken by press photographer Georg Pahl (*20.10.1900; +13.5.1963), who in 1923 founded the "Fotoagentur A-B-C-Aktuelle-Bilder-Centrale, Georg Pahl" in Berlin.

[All documents of this inventory](https://www.bild.bundesarchiv.de/dba/en/search/?topicid%5B%5D=dcx-dcxapi%3Atm_topic/thes_bestand_774u70q3f9s1mwledd48 "All documents of this inventory")

![Image 3: Bild 101 Wehrmacht Propaganda Troops (=Propagandakompanien der Wehrmacht)](https://bild.bundesarchiv.de/device_barch/dev1/2024/04-16/d5/2e/file7v0vpfr3lfrn5doveil.jpg)

The fonds is divided into three parts: "Army and Air Force" (Bild 101 I), "Navy" (Bild 101 II) and "Waffen-SS" (Bild 101 III). The photographs of the so-called "Bildberichter[a1]", i.e. mostly professional photographers in the service of the Wehrmacht and the Waffen-SS, show the different branches of the armed forces in the various war zones. After being censored by the Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda, the photos were sent to German and foreign news agencies for publication.

[All documents of this inventory](https://www.bild.bundesarchiv.de/dba/en/search/?topicid%5B%5D=dcx-dcxapi%3Atm_topic/thes_bestand_774u70q3f5w1n3n6cd48 "All documents of this inventory")

![Image 4: Bild 183 Allgemeiner Deutscher Nachrichtendienst - Zentralbild (=General German News Service)](https://bild.bundesarchiv.de/device_barch/dev1/2024/05-14/ed/e3/file7vf7p75rq09tfzu51u1.jpg)

Among the approx. 5.5 million pictures of this record group there are mainly photos of the GDR picture agency "ADN/Zentralbild", which represent the life in the GDR from a quasi-official point of view. Apart from these photos there are also photos from the Scherl picture archive dating back to the German Empire and photos of Wehrmacht propaganda companies kept in this record group.

[All documents of this inventory](https://www.bild.bundesarchiv.de/dba/en/search/?topicid%5B%5D=dcx-dcxapi%3Atm_topic/thes_bestand_774u70q3gbp1k44ckd48 "All documents of this inventory")

![Image 5: B 145 Bild Federal Press and Information Office (Presse- und Informationsamt der Bundesregierung.- Bildbestand)](https://bild.bundesarchiv.de/device_barch/dev1/2024/06-14/27/b0/file7vv726qr16rqs523283.jpg)

The record group "B 145 Bild" contains approx. 1.1 million photographs documenting the political, economic, social and "architectural" life of the Federal Republic of Germany until the 1990s. Some of the pictures date back to the German Empire, the Weimar Republic and the National Socialist period.

[All documents of this inventory](https://www.bild.bundesarchiv.de/dba/en/search/?topicid%5B%5D=dcx-dcxapi%3Atm_topic/thes_bestand_774u70q3emh1mmlk9d48 "All documents of this inventory")

32.title: Landscapes of Continuity and Change in the West Usambara Mountains, c. 1910 · USU Digital Exhibits
32.content:
Welcome to the Usambara Public History Project Digital Exhibit. The exhibit contains early twentieth century landscape photographs from Walther Dobbertin, a professional photographer resident in German East Africa from approximately 1903 to 1914. In addition to Dobbertin’s images, the Usambara Project team located and photographed several of the original landscapes in 2016 and 2019.

In addition to their depictions of German life in East Africa, the exhibit’s images argue for Africans carrying out an ecological restoration project using time tested techniques that conserved soil and relied on a diverse set of exotic and indigenous plants.

### The Larger Project

The exhibit forms part of the Usambara Landscape History Project, which aims to document the history of landscape transformation across the Usambara Mountains of North-eastern Tanzania. Collaborators include the Mlalo Elder’s Council, The Usambara Elder’s Council, Utah State University Libraries' Digital Initiatives Unit, Utah State University Libraries' Special Collections & Archives Department, Kivatiro Hamza Kitojo, Sufian Shekoloa (marehemu) and Chris Conte, Professor, Utah State University.

### Work to Date

*   2016 –Located the sites of the Dobbertin landscapes and conducted preliminary interviews to determine the project’s feasibility.
*   2019 –Conducted group interview sessions at Mlalo, Gare, Kwefingo, and Vuga over the month of July.

### Upcoming Work

*   2022 –Complete and show physical exhibit.
*   2022 –Complete first iteration of the digital exhibit.
*   2022 –Agroforestry stories, mapping, and inventories.
*   2022 –Identify new projects and invite new team members.
